paragraphs: Gradient-based meta-reinforcement learning trains a learner at two levels: an inner loop adapts to a task, while an outer loop learns how to make that adaptation effective. This paper develops a common framework for analyzing these methods and shows that their existing stochastic meta-gradient estimates are biased. The issue concerns the direction of the learning signal, beyond random variation between estimates.

The analysis separates two sources of bias. One comes from composing the outer objective with estimated inner updates; its bound depends on the number of updates, learning rate, estimation variance, and sample size. The other comes from Hessian estimates produced through automatic differentiation across multiple steps. These errors can propagate into the outer gradient, with a polynomial dependence described by the analysis.

Experiments with tabular decision processes provide quantitative support for the theory. Further experiments on Iterated Prisoner's Dilemma and Atari games illustrate how off-policy learning and lower-bias estimators can help address the problem. The contribution connects identifiable estimation errors to practical choices in meta-learning algorithms.
neurips-2022-a-theoretical-understanding.tldr: The paper identifies two sources of gradient bias in meta-reinforcement learning and shows how alternative estimation methods can help reduce them.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to recover an unknown classifier’s labels exactly on a finite collection of points while asking relatively few questions. It covers both two-class and multiclass problems. Its geometric assumption is a new separation measure called strong convex hull margin, which extends the margin used in support vector machines.

The central challenge is balancing the number of questions against the computation needed to choose them. With ordinary label queries alone, the worst-case query requirement grows sharply with dimension and inverse margin. More powerful seed queries, a variant of equivalence queries, allow Littlestone’s Halving algorithm to use O(m log n) queries, but that algorithm is computationally inefficient.

The authors show that carefully combining both query types achieves polynomial running time in the number of points n and dimension m. For binary classification, their method uses O(m² log n) label queries and O(m log(m/γ)) seed queries, where γ is the margin. This establishes that a mixture of queries can support both computational efficiency and controlled query counts.

The result extends to k classes with a k!k² multiplicative overhead. Similar guarantees hold for bounded-bit-complexity inputs or when just one class has the required margin against the others. A complementary worst-case lower bound of Ω(km log(1/γ)) on seed and label queries shows that some dependence on class count, dimension, and margin is unavoidable.
neurips-2022-active-learning-of-classifi.tldr: Combining label and seed queries enables exact learning of classifiers under a geometric margin assumption with polynomial computation and provable query bounds.

paragraphs: Meta-learning aims to prepare a learner for new tasks by training it across other tasks. Its success on existing benchmarks relies on training tasks covering the kinds of tasks encountered at test time. When available tasks are too few or too similar, the learner can memorize them or overfit to their narrow distribution.

Adversarial Task Up-sampling, or ATU, addresses this problem by generating additional tasks from task representations using a dedicated network. The generation process maximizes an adversarial loss to produce tasks intended to contribute strongly to the current meta-learner. This makes task creation responsive to the learner as it changes, tying augmentation to its present learning needs.

The authors evaluate ATU on few-shot sine regression and image classification datasets. They report marked improvements over leading task augmentation strategies in both meta-test performance and the quality of generated tasks. These findings support learner-dependent task generation as a way to improve the usefulness of limited training tasks in the evaluated settings.
neurips-2022-adversarial-task-up-samplin.tldr: ATU generates additional tasks through an adversarial objective, improving few-shot meta-learning in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: The lottery ticket hypothesis concerns sparse subnetworks that can train successfully from their original initial weights. Iterative magnitude pruning searches for these winning tickets. In deep networks such as ResNet, this process does not work well with a large initial learning rate, creating a puzzle because large initial rates generally help optimization reach flatter minima.

The authors investigate whether winning tickets instead occupy relatively sharp minima. Their experiments confirm this behavior for iterative magnitude pruning with a small learning rate. They also find that distance from the initial weights is closely involved in winning tickets, suggesting that sharpness alone does not explain their generalization behavior.

To connect these observations, the paper develops a PAC-Bayesian bound using a spike-and-slab distribution, a formulation suited to sparse networks. This provides an explicit theoretical perspective on how lottery tickets and generalization relate. The authors then revisit existing ticket-finding algorithms through that perspective, using both the sharpness findings and the role of initialization to develop new interpretations.
neurips-2022-analyzing-lottery-ticket-hy.tldr: A PAC-Bayesian analysis connects winning tickets’ generalization to their relatively sharp minima and relationship to initialization.

paragraphs: Neural architecture search automates decisions about a network's structure, but exploring many possibilities can be expensive. A common shortcut searches for one building block and repeats it throughout the network. This reduces the search space while restricting how much different parts of the final model can vary.

BLOX supports studying a broader macro search space, where blocks within one network can differ. The benchmark contains 91,000 distinct models trained on CIFAR-100, together with runtime measurements across diverse hardware platforms. These measurements allow researchers to examine predictive performance alongside how a model runs on different devices.

The authors use the benchmark to compare established algorithms studied in cell-based search spaces with emerging blockwise methods designed to scale to larger macro spaces. The contribution is a shared basis for investigating those approaches systematically. It responds to evidence that allowing different blocks can improve performance, while making the resulting search problem available for direct algorithm comparisons.
neurips-2022-blox-macro-neural-architect.tldr: BLOX provides 91,000 trained models and hardware runtime measurements for studying architecture search with different blocks within a network.

paragraphs: This paper develops a way to certify model performance under distribution changes constrained by fairness requirements. It formulates certification as an optimization problem: bound the model's loss on distributions that satisfy those requirements and remain within a bounded distance of the training distribution. The certificate therefore depends on an explicitly restricted set of possible shifts.

The proposed framework handles both sensitive shifting and more general shifting scenarios. Its main computational strategy divides the original distribution into subpopulations that can be analyzed separately. The authors prove convexity of the resulting subproblems, making this decomposition a mathematical route to solving the certification problem.

Across six real-world datasets, the authors report tight certificates for sensitive shifting and non-trivial certificates for general shifting. Adding non-skewness constraints can tighten the bounds further. Comparisons on Gaussian data also produce substantially tighter bounds than adapted distributional robustness methods. These results show how structured assumptions about distribution changes can yield informative fairness-related performance guarantees.
neurips-2022-certifying-some-distributio.tldr: Subpopulation decomposition enables performance certificates over nearby distributions subject to fairness constraints.

paragraphs: Prediction intervals for collections of time series face two distinct coverage questions. At a particular time, they should cover outcomes across the population. Across time, they should also cover outcomes for each individual series. For patient monitoring, these correspond to reliability across patients and reliability throughout one patient's trajectory.

Temporal Quantile Adjustment, or TQA, modifies conformal prediction to account for both questions. Conformal methods typically construct intervals using a fixed quantile of calibration nonconformity scores. TQA instead adjusts which quantile is queried at each time step, with a theoretically grounded treatment of cross-sectional and longitudinal coverage.

Because this adjustment happens after prediction, TQA can wrap any time-series regression model. The experiments generally find efficient intervals and improved longitudinal coverage while maintaining cross-sectional coverage. The contribution is a method for addressing the two dimensions of reliability together: good population-wide coverage at individual times does not by itself describe coverage over each series' history.
neurips-2022-conformal-prediction-with-t.tldr: TQA adjusts conformal quantiles over time to improve coverage along individual series while preserving coverage across the population.

paragraphs: This paper studies how distributional reinforcement learning can learn policies optimized for the CVaR risk measure. Modeling a distribution of outcomes provides information relevant to risk-sensitive decisions, but the authors show that the usual action-selection procedure does not necessarily optimize the intended CVaR objective. Representing outcome uncertainty and choosing actions consistently with a risk objective are separate challenges.

Specifically, standard action selection with the distributional Bellman optimality operator can converge to neither dynamic, Markovian CVaR nor static, non-Markovian CVaR. The authors respond by modifying existing algorithms, including introducing a new distributional Bellman operator. These changes expand the ability of distributional methods to learn and represent CVaR-optimized policies.

The approach is a simple extension of standard distributional reinforcement learning algorithms, allowing it to benefit from advances in deep reinforcement learning. Experiments on synthetic and real data show better CVaR-optimized policies. The findings establish both a failure mode in conventional action selection and an empirically supported way to address it.
neurips-2022-distributional-reinforcemen.tldr: Modified distributional reinforcement learning updates address a failure of standard action selection to optimize CVaR risk objectives.

paragraphs: This paper examines whether adding self-supervised learning objectives improves online reinforcement learning from images. The authors extend a framework that jointly trains self-supervised and reinforcement learning losses, then test many self-supervised objectives. Their comparisons hold the amount of data and image augmentation equal, helping isolate the contribution of the extra learning losses.

Under those comparisons, the existing joint-training framework does not produce meaningful improvements over baselines using image augmentation alone. The authors also use evolutionary search to find combinations of self-supervised losses. Even these searched combinations fail to meaningfully outperform methods using carefully designed augmentations in the reported experiments.

Evaluation spans multiple environments, including a real robot environment, and finds that no tested loss or augmentation dominates everywhere. Additional ablations examine contributing factors and the representations learned by different approaches. The results question the benefits of the studied joint-optimization framework and emphasize that augmentation choices and environment differences matter when judging gains from self-supervised objectives.
neurips-2022-does-self-supervised-learni.tldr: With data and augmentation matched, tested self-supervised objectives did not meaningfully improve pixel-based reinforcement learning over augmentation-only baselines.

paragraphs: Continuous-time gradient flow is often easier to analyze than the discrete, noisy updates of stochastic gradient descent. This paper asks when convergence results for gradient flow on population loss can establish convergence for practical optimization methods. Its answer is conditional: convergence of the continuous process must come with additional structure.

The central tool is a converse Lyapunov-style theorem. Under mild assumptions on gradient flow's convergence rates, it establishes a potential function that can track progress. These potentials yield a correspondence between convergence rates and geometric properties of the objective. When they also satisfy self-bounding properties, they support convergence guarantees for gradient descent and stochastic gradient descent.

The argument does not require the discrete algorithms to follow paths close to gradient flow. The authors also show that the self-bounding requirements are, in a qualified sense, necessary. Their framework unifies analyses of convex objectives, objectives with PL or KL properties, and problems including phase retrieval and matrix square roots.
neurips-2022-from-gradient-flow-on-popul.tldr: Lyapunov potentials connect gradient-flow convergence to guarantees for gradient descent and SGD when additional self-bounding conditions hold.

paragraphs: Reconstructing a person in 3D from a few noisy RGBD views can lose both fine detail and overall geometric consistency. The paper identifies a particular problem in PIFu-based methods: their representations can amplify depth noise, producing flattened faces and faulty body geometry. It targets reconstruction from sparse, noisy captures.

The proposed method trains depth denoising and 3D reconstruction together so that each task informs the other. Denoising supplies richer local geometry to reconstruction features, while reconstruction contributes information about global topology to denoising. This reciprocal relationship aims to improve the inputs and representations used to recover the person.

A two-scale PIFu representation then uses two multilayer perceptrons with denoised depth and geometry-aware features. The scales separately address detailed facial structure and consistent body reconstruction. Experiments show improved reconstruction of faces and bodies in different poses, outperforming the compared state-of-the-art methods. The approach connects noise handling with the differing geometric demands of facial detail and whole-body shape.
neurips-2022-geometry-aware-two-scale-pi.tldr: Joint depth denoising and two-scale reconstruction improve facial detail and body geometry from sparse, noisy RGBD inputs.

paragraphs: Sparse training can reduce training and inference costs by removing parameters, but it commonly produces one model with a fixed computational footprint. That is restrictive when available hardware resources change after training. Dynamic inference addresses this by providing several subnetworks that perform the same task at different computational costs.

Training those subnetworks together traditionally introduces substantial overhead through joint optimization. Alternating Sparse Training, or AST, instead trains multiple sparse subnetworks without extra training cost relative to training a single sparse model from scratch. A gradient correction procedure within inner-group iterations reduces interference between the subnetworks' weight updates.

Across multiple datasets, AST achieves similar or better accuracy than the compared sparse training methods while producing subnetworks with several sparsity levels in one training run. Compared with traditional joint training for dynamic inference, the authors report eliminating its large overhead without reducing individual subnetwork accuracy. The result makes post-training adjustment of computation compatible with the reported cost of training one sparse model.
neurips-2022-get-more-at-once-alternatin.tldr: AST trains multiple sparse subnetworks at the reported cost of training one, using gradient correction to reduce update interference.

paragraphs: Sequencing produces mixtures of noisy genome fragments, and reconstructing their constituent sequences requires disentangling which fragments belong together. For chromosomes, this is the haplotype assembly problem; related techniques recover different viral strains, or quasispecies. The task becomes harder in polyploid organisms, which have more than two chromosome copies.

The authors argue that existing neural approaches inadequately model relationships among the reads, even though those relationships are important for separating the mixture. Their method, NeurHap, combines graph representation learning with combinatorial optimization. The paper's graph-coloring approach brings a discrete organization problem together with learned representations of read relationships.

Experiments on both real and synthetic datasets show substantially better performance than competing approaches. The contribution is therefore a combination of relational modeling and structured optimization for an NP-hard reconstruction problem. Its stated results support treating interactions among reads as a central part of recovering genetic components from noisy sequencing mixtures.
neurips-2022-graph-coloring-via-neural-n.tldr: NeurHap combines graph learning and combinatorial optimization to improve reconstruction of chromosome copies and viral strains from noisy reads.

paragraphs: When an action-recognition model learns new classes over time, storing examples of earlier classes can reduce catastrophic forgetting. Videos consume substantial memory, however, so a limited storage budget permits only a small collection. FrameMaker addresses this bottleneck by learning a compact representation for each selected video.

Its Frame Condensing component preserves one learned condensed frame in place of the full video. A second component, the Instance-Specific Prompt, aims to compensate for spatial and temporal details lost during condensation. Together, these components seek to retain information useful for later incremental tasks while sharply reducing storage requirements.

On HMDB51, UCF101, and Something-Something V2, the authors report better performance than recent advanced methods while using only 20% of their memory. They also report substantial improvements when methods receive the same memory budget. These comparisons support learned condensation as a useful way to preserve prior video knowledge under storage constraints, with prompts helping address the information lost by reducing a sequence to one frame.
neurips-2022-learning-a-condensed-frame-.tldr: FrameMaker stores a learned condensed frame and compensating prompt per selected video, improving incremental action recognition with much less memory.

paragraphs: Visual Transformers process tokens derived from image patches, but these operations do not explicitly teach them how viewpoints relate through 3D structure. Models trained on collections of 2D images can consequently struggle with unfamiliar camera views. This paper introduces a layer intended to make viewpoint changes more directly accessible to the representation.

The 3D Token Representation Layer, or 3DTRL, estimates tokens' 3D positions using a pseudo-depth estimator and a learned camera matrix. Trained without supervision for this process, these components impose geometric transformations on tokens recovered from 2D patches. The resulting positional information supports learning representations that are less tied to a particular viewpoint.

The layer can be inserted into a Transformer with minimal additional computation. In experiments on image classification, multi-view video alignment, and action recognition, models containing 3DTRL outperform their corresponding backbone Transformers across the evaluated tasks. These results support adding estimated 3D structure as a useful representation component across several types of visual understanding.
neurips-2022-learning-viewpoint-agnostic.tldr: 3DTRL adds estimated 3D token positions to Transformers, improving the evaluated visual tasks with minimal extra computation.

paragraphs: Sharpness-Aware Minimization, or SAM, trains a network to resist increases in loss caused by perturbing its weights. This encourages a smoother loss landscape, but perturbing every parameter introduces substantial computation. The authors find that applying these perturbations indiscriminately is also suboptimal for the learning procedure.

Sparse SAM, or SSAM, uses a binary mask to select which weights receive perturbations. The paper offers two ways to construct the mask, based on Fisher information and dynamic sparse training. This makes the perturbation sparse; the central modification concerns where SAM probes the loss landscape during training.

The authors prove a convergence rate matching SAM's O(log T/√T) rate. Experiments on CIFAR10, CIFAR100, and ImageNet-1K show greater efficiency than SAM while maintaining or improving performance with 50% perturbation sparsity. Together, the theoretical and empirical results indicate that perturbing fewer parameters can preserve the method's benefits while reducing its computational burden in the evaluated settings.
neurips-2022-make-sharpness-aware-minimi.tldr: Sparse SAM selectively perturbs weights, matching SAM's stated convergence rate and improving experimental efficiency while preserving or improving performance.

paragraphs: Decoding electroencephalographic signals is central to non-invasive brain-computer interfaces. Deep learning has improved decoding performance, while geometric learning has attracted interest for its robustness to noisy EEG data. This paper investigates how to combine these approaches within one model, addressing a relatively underexplored connection between neural networks and geometric EEG representations.

The proposed manifold attention network, mAtt, uses an attention mechanism that characterizes spatial and temporal EEG information on a Riemannian manifold of symmetric positive definite representations. Its distinguishing design choice is to perform this representation learning fully within that geometric setting. Attention and geometric structure are therefore integrated into the same decoding mechanism.

Evaluations on both time-synchronous and time-asynchronous EEG datasets suggest better performance than other leading deep-learning methods. Interpretability analysis also indicates that mAtt captures informative features and handles changes in brain dynamics over time. These results support the combined geometric and neural approach for the evaluated EEG decoding settings.
neurips-2022-matt-a-manifold-attention-n.tldr: mAtt combines attention with geometric EEG representations, with evaluations suggesting improved decoding and useful handling of changing brain dynamics.

paragraphs: Optimization algorithms can favor particular solutions even when many models fit the training data. This implicit bias matters for understanding generalization. The paper studies which solutions are selected by a family of mirror-descent algorithms whose potential is the p-th power of the ℓp norm, calling the family p-GD.

For linearly separable classification, the authors prove that p-GD converges in direction to a generalized maximum-margin solution measured with the ℓp norm. The qualification about direction is central: the result characterizes the orientation of the learned classifier. It connects the optimizer's chosen geometry with the separating solution that training favors.

The paper also addresses implementation cost. Although general mirror-descent updates can be expensive, p-GD can be fully parallelized like SGD and used for deep networks with virtually no extra computational overhead. Experiments with linear models and deep networks show noticeable effects on learned structure and generalization. These empirical findings extend the practical investigation beyond the separable setting covered by the directional theorem.
neurips-2022-mirror-descent-maximizes-ge.tldr: For linearly separable classification, p-GD converges toward an ℓp maximum-margin direction and supports efficient parallel implementation.

paragraphs: Variational inequalities provide one mathematical framework for minimization, games, saddle points, and equilibrium problems. This paper studies their stochastic, sum-type form in decentralized systems, where computation is distributed across a network. It covers both fixed networks and networks whose connections change over time.

The authors establish lower complexity bounds for two distinct resources: communication between participants and local computational iterations. They then construct algorithms that match those bounds. This pairing is what supports the optimality claim: within the studied setting, the algorithms attain the stated limits for the resources being analyzed.

The paper also reports that its algorithms improve on available complexity results in decentralized deterministic and non-distributed stochastic cases. Experiments support their effectiveness. The contribution combines a description of unavoidable costs with methods that achieve them, giving a common theoretical treatment to several related optimization settings and clarifying how communication and local work enter decentralized solution methods.
neurips-2022-optimal-algorithms-for-dece.tldr: The paper develops decentralized variational-inequality algorithms that match lower bounds on communication and local iteration complexity.

paragraphs: Fine-grained categories can share nearly all their parts while differing in how those parts relate to the overall object. Recognizing the parts alone can therefore leave the key distinction unresolved. This paper focuses on relationships between local views and global structure as information for identifying such closely related categories.

The authors formalize what it means for fine-grained categories to be distinguishable and prove necessary and sufficient conditions for learning their decision boundaries within that setting. They use those theoretical findings to design Relational Proxies, an approach that encodes semantic labels through relationships between an object's global and local views.

Evaluation on seven fine-grained benchmark datasets produces state-of-the-art results on all seven, with improvements exceeding 4% in some cases. Additional experiments yield results consistent with the distinguishability theory across multiple benchmarks. The contribution links a formal account of what makes these categories separable with a practical method for representing the relevant relationships.
neurips-2022-relational-proxies-emergent.tldr: Relational Proxies uses relationships between local parts and global structure to distinguish fine-grained categories, guided by a formal distinguishability analysis.

paragraphs: Microservice applications consist of many interacting components, making it difficult to locate the origin of a failure quickly. This paper proposes a scalable root-cause analysis algorithm based on causal discovery. Its starting point is to treat a failure as an intervention on the component or variable responsible for it.

The algorithm learns only the portion of the causal graph relevant to the suspected root cause and explores the graph hierarchically. This localized strategy avoids many costly conditional independence tests that broader causal discovery would require. The approach relies on diagnostic data and is designed to work across applications.

The authors compare it with a modified PC algorithm and a leading root-cause analysis method. Their results show considerably better top-k recall and substantially shorter execution time. These findings support focusing causal learning on the part of the system needed for diagnosis, allowing useful root-cause information to be recovered where traditional techniques become computationally impractical.
neurips-2022-root-cause-analysis-of-fail.tldr: Hierarchical, localized causal discovery improves microservice root-cause detection while reducing the computation required for diagnosis.

paragraphs: TANGO changes the rendered appearance of an existing 3D shape according to a text description. It targets photorealistic stylization of surface meshes with arbitrary topology, including bare or low-quality meshes. The method uses supervision from CLIP to connect the text prompt with the visual appearance produced by rendering.

Its central design separates appearance into spatially varying reflectance, local geometric variation, and lighting. These components are optimized jointly through a differentiable renderer based on spherical Gaussians. Separating them gives the optimization explicit ways to account for how surface properties, geometry, and illumination contribute to the final image.

The method predicts reflectance effects without training on a task-specific dataset. Experiments report better photorealistic quality, 3D geometric consistency, and robustness on low-quality meshes than existing text-driven style-transfer methods. The findings support decomposing the rendering process as a useful way to turn language guidance into a coherent appearance for a given 3D object.
neurips-2022-tango-text-driven-photoreal.tldr: TANGO jointly optimizes reflectance, local geometry, and lighting to give existing 3D meshes photorealistic appearances guided by text.

paragraphs: Federated neural-network training can perform much worse than centralized training when clients have dissimilar data. This paper attributes much of that gap to nonconvex optimization challenges. The authors find that early network layers learn useful features, while later layers fail to use those features effectively under federated optimization.

Train-Convexify-Train, or TCT, turns that observation into a two-stage training procedure separated by a change in the optimization problem. It first learns features using an existing federated method such as FedAvg. It then forms a convex approximation using the network's empirical neural tangent kernel and optimizes that problem.

This procedure preserves the opportunity to learn useful features before applying the convex formulation. On clients with dissimilar data, the authors report accuracy improvements of up to +36% on FMNIST and +37% on CIFAR10. The results support nonconvex optimization difficulties as a substantial contributor to the observed performance gap and show a practical way to address them in the evaluated settings.
neurips-2022-tct-convexifying-federated-.tldr: TCT first learns federated features and then optimizes a convex kernel approximation, improving accuracy when clients have dissimilar data.

paragraphs: This paper proposes a text classifier inspired by quantum physics' idea of superposition. It treats a document as a superposition of its words and derives a corresponding wave function. Born's rule then supplies the probability of a transition from the document representation to a target class, forming the basis of classification.

The authors present two complementary implementations of the same idea. One calculates the wave functions explicitly, making that mathematical representation part of the direct computation. The other places the classifier inside a neural-network architecture. These implementations offer two ways to operationalize the connection between document representation and class probabilities.

Analysis on three benchmark datasets examines classification performance, explainability, and computational efficiency. The abstract presents this as an investigation of those properties without claiming a specific performance advantage. It also states that the ideas apply beyond text. The main contribution is a quantum-inspired formulation of classification together with explicit and neural implementations for studying its practical behavior.
neurips-2022-text-classification-with-bo.tldr: The paper represents documents as word superpositions and uses Born's rule to compute class probabilities through explicit or neural implementations.

paragraphs: Large vision-language models can transfer well to new tasks, but pretraining them requires substantial data and computation. BeamCLIP addresses a different part of that process: transferring representations from an already trained CLIP-ViT teacher into a smaller model such as ResNet-18. The aim is to make the teacher's learned representation useful within a compact model.

For unsupervised transfer, cross-modal similarity matching teaches the student to match the teacher's relative similarity distribution across text-prompt embeddings. This uses relationships to language representations as the training signal. Context-based prompt augmentation improves the encoding of those prompts by reducing ambiguity in their wording.

In the reported ImageNet-1K linear-probe evaluation, the transferred ResNet-18 reaches 66.2% top-1 accuracy, compared with 51.8% for SimCLR and 63.7% for SwAV. It also approaches the stated supervised result of 69.8%. These findings show that unsupervised transfer from a pretrained vision-language teacher can produce stronger small-model representations than the compared vision-only self-supervised methods.
neurips-2022-transferring-pre-trained-mu.tldr: BeamCLIP transfers a large vision-language teacher's representations into a smaller model by matching similarities to text prompts.
